title: Prosecutor v. Milan Martić — shelling of Zagreb
question: Did the shelling of Zagreb on 2 and 3 May 1995 constitute attacks on civilians in violation of the laws or customs of war?
facts: In the early morning of 1 May 1995, Croatian armed forces launched Operation Flash in Western Slavonia in the RSK. Negotiations took place during the operation, and agreements were reached on 3 May. The operation ended around 4 May, after which a large part of the Serb population fled Western Slavonia. At 1:00 p.m. on 1 May, Milan Celeketic ordered artillery fire on Sisak near Zagreb in the accused's presence. The same day, an M-87 Orkan unit was moved from the Knin area to Vojnic, about 50 kilometres south of Zagreb. On the morning of 2 May, without warning, Orkan rockets struck Zagreb's main square, shopping streets, a school, Pleso near the airport, and the airport; five civilians were killed and at least 160 people were severely injured. At midday on 3 May, Orkan rockets struck the Croatian National Theatre at Marshal Tito Square, a children's hospital, and another square; two people were killed and 54 injured. The M-87 Orkan launched non-guided rockets. The primary use of the M-87 Orkan is to target soldiers and armoured vehicles. Each rocket used in the attacks contained a cluster warhead with 288 bomblets; each bomblet released 420 steel pellets on impact, with a lethal range of 10 metres. At a range of 50 kilometres the system had a targeting error of one kilometre in any direction. The rockets were fired from the Vojnic area near Slavsko Polje, at the extreme of the weapon's range. The Defence identified the Ministry of the Interior, the Ministry of Defence, Zagreb airport, and the Presidential Palace as military targets in Zagreb. The Defence also argued that the attacks were reprisals for Croatian forces' conduct during Operation Flash.
holding: In its Trial Judgment of 12 June 2007, the ICTY Trial Chamber found Milan Martić guilty under Article 7(1) of the Statute on Zagreb-related Counts 15 (murder, a crime against humanity), 17 (inhumane acts, a crime against humanity), and 19 (attacks on civilians, a violation of the laws or customs of war). It found him not guilty on Count 2, extermination. It found the elements of murder and cruel treatment under Counts 16 and 18 established, but treated those crimes as absorbed by Count 19 and entered no separate convictions on them. The Chamber imposed a single sentence of 35 years' imprisonment for the convictions in the judgment; it was not a sentence only for the Zagreb shelling.
key_reasoning: The M-87 Orkan's characteristics and the firing range used in the attacks meant it could not hit specific targets; its use in a densely populated civilian area would cause severe casualties.
The Defence's identified military targets did not alter the Chamber's assessment in light of the weapon's characteristics.
The evidence did not establish the conditions for lawful reprisals, including that the attacks were a last resort or that a prior formal warning had been given.
